opus-5.5.text:
I think we get there the same way we came to understand most complicated systems: by building better instruments and doing a lot of careful, unglamorous science. Right now interpretability is a bit like biology before good microscopes. We have hints of structure inside these models, things like features, circuits, and directions in activation space that seem to correspond to concepts, but we're still figuring out what the right units of analysis even are.

A few things have to come together. First, we need decompositions that are faithful to what the model is actually computing, not just stories that look plausible to us. Methods like sparse autoencoders were a big step because they let us pull apart superposition and find features that are more interpretable than individual neurons. But they're lossy, so a lot of the frontier work is about closing that gap: how much of the model's behavior can you actually explain with the features you've found?

Second, understanding has to be causal, not just descriptive. It's not enough to say "this feature lights up on deception." You want to be able to intervene, turn it up or down, and predict what the model will do. When you can edit a model's behavior in a precise, predictable way, that's when I start to believe we understand something.

Third, and this is the part I'm most excited about, it has to scale, and that means automation. Frontier models have billions of features and enormously complex interactions. No team of humans is going to label all of that by hand. So I think AI systems themselves will do much of the interpretation work: proposing hypotheses about what a component does, running experiments, and checking explanations against real behavior. Humans set the standards and audit the results.

And last, I think the real test is usefulness. We'll know we're confident when interpretability lets us do things we couldn't do otherwise: catch a failure mode before deployment, remove a capability surgically, or fix a bug in a model the way you'd fix a bug in code. Once it becomes a practical engineering discipline rather than a collection of interesting findings, I think that's when we can honestly say we understand what's going on inside.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers are still figuring out the right units of analysis and describes decomposing computation into features, suggesting the fundamental units may need to be reconceived.

r002.rationale: The response gives no prediction that confident understanding will be achieved in 2028.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about constantly, and I want to be honest that my answer has changed over the last couple of years.

When I started, I believed the path to confidence was essentially a path to completeness. You'd decompose the network into features, map the features into circuits, and eventually you'd have something like a wiring diagram you could read top to bottom. Confidence would come from coverage. If you'd accounted for everything, you'd understand it.

I no longer think that's how it's going to go, at least not on the timeline that matters. The models are growing faster than our ability to enumerate them, and frankly, even when we do find clean circuits, they explain a slice of the behavior rather than the whole thing. Chasing full coverage starts to feel like trying to understand a city by cataloguing every brick.

So the framing I've moved toward is closer to how we trust things in biology or engineering. Confidence doesn't come from a complete account. It comes from making predictions that could have failed and watching them not fail. If I claim a particular feature represents, say, deception or sycophancy, the test isn't whether the story is elegant. It's whether I can intervene on it, turn it up or down, and get the behavioral change I predicted in advance. And then whether that holds up on inputs I didn't pick.

The second piece is that you need multiple independent lines of evidence converging. Sparse dictionary methods say one thing, attribution methods say something consistent, behavioral probes agree, and you can reproduce it across model scales. Any one of those alone, I'd distrust. Together, they start to constrain the space of possible explanations in a way that feels like real knowledge.

And the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that we need adversarial pressure on our own interpretations. Right now most interpretability results are produced by the people who have an incentive for them to look good. We need the equivalent of red-teaming for explanations. Build a model where you know the ground truth because you planted it, then see if the tools recover it. Have someone else try to break your circuit story. If an explanation survives people actively trying to falsify it, that's when I'd start saying we understand something.

So my short answer is: not through completeness, but through a growing body of interventions, predictions, and failed attempts to falsify, accumulating the way understanding accumulates in any empirical science. It'll feel less like reading source code and more like gradually trusting a theory. I think that's fine. It's actually the only kind of understanding that's ever worked for complex systems.

astra-6.text:
I think confidence will come from being able to test our explanations. If we think a network is using a particular mechanism, can we predict when that mechanism will activate, what happens if we remove it, and how the model’s behavior changes if we modify it? Then we need to see whether those predictions hold on examples we haven’t already studied.

A compelling visualization can give us a hypothesis. But the stronger evidence is that we can intervene and get the result we expected. I suspect understanding will build up that way: small, testable explanations that eventually fit together into a larger picture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think confidence will come from being able to make predictions and then test them. If we think a particular part of a network is doing something, we should be able to intervene on it and predict how the network’s behavior will change. And that explanation should hold up across different inputs, rather than just explaining a few examples after the fact.

There’s also a question of what level of understanding we need. Understanding every individual parameter may be less useful than discovering principles that explain how the network represents information and uses it. I’d expect progress to involve moving between those levels: detailed studies of particular mechanisms, and broader theories that tell us when those mechanisms should appear. When those approaches start making reliable predictions that agree with each other, I think we’ll have a much stronger basis for confidence.
